'''Margaret Mary Beckett, Baroness Beckett''' (''{{nee}}'' '''Jackson'''; born 15 January 1943) is a British politician who was the United Kingdom's first female [[Foreign Secretary (United Kingdom)|Foreign Secretary]] (from 2006 to 2007) and  a [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|member of Parliament]] (MP) for more than 45 years, first from 1974 to 1979 and then from 1983 to 2024. A member of the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]], she served as a minister under Prime Ministers [[Harold Wilson]], [[James Callaghan]], [[Tony Blair]] and [[Gordon Brown]]. Beckett was [[Deputy Leader of the Opposition]] and [[Deputy Leader of the Labour Party (UK)|Deputy Leader of the Labour Party]] from 1992 to 1994, and briefly [[Leader of the Opposition (United Kingdom)|Leader of the Opposition]] and acting [[Leader of the Labour Party (UK)|Leader of the Labour Party]] following [[John Smith (Labour Party leader)|John Smith]]'s death in 1994. A member of the Labour Party, she served as MP for [[Lincoln (constituency)|Lincoln]] from 1974 to 1979, and for [[Derby South]] from 1983 to 2024. Her 45 years in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] makes her the female MP in the Commons with the longest service overall ([[Harriet Harman]] has longer continuous service), and she was the last sitting MP who served in the Labour governments of the 1970s.

Beckett was first elected to [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|Parliament]] at the [[October 1974 United Kingdom general election|October 1974 general election]] for Lincoln and held junior positions in the governments of Harold Wilson and James Callaghan. She lost her seat at the [[1979 United Kingdom general election|1979 general election]], but returned to the Commons in 1983 as MP for Derby South. She was appointed to [[Neil Kinnock]]'s [[Kinnock shadow cabinet|shadow cabinet]] shortly afterwards; she was elected Deputy Leader of the Labour Party in 1992, becoming the first woman to hold that role. When [[John Smith (Labour Party leader)|John Smith]] died in 1994, Beckett became the first woman to lead the Labour Party, though only in a temporary capacity—Blair won the [[1994 Labour Party leadership election|election to replace Smith]] shortly afterward and assumed the substantive leadership.

After Labour returned to power in 1997, and as one of [[Blair Babes|101 female Labour MPs elected]], Beckett became a member of Blair's [[Cabinet of the United Kingdom|Cabinet]] initially as [[President of the Board of Trade]], the first female holder of that office. She later served as [[Leader of the House of Commons]] and [[Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs]], before becoming Foreign Secretary in 2006, the first woman to hold that position, and—after [[Margaret Thatcher]]—the second woman to hold one of the [[Great Offices of State]]. Following Blair's resignation as [[Prime Minister of the United Kingdom|prime minister]] in 2007, Beckett was not initially given a position by Brown, Blair's successor; after she had spent a period on the backbenches, Brown appointed her to his cabinet as [[Minister of State for Housing and Planning]] in 2008, before she left the government for the last time in 2009. After Labour lost power following the [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010 general election]], she sat on the opposition backbenches until standing down at the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]]. She was shortly thereafter appointed to the [[House of Lords]].

==Early life==
Margaret Beckett was born Margaret Mary Jackson in 1943, in [[Ashton-under-Lyne]], Lancashire, into the family of a disabled  Congregationalist carpenter father and an Irish Catholic teacher mother. Her father died early, precipitating family [[poverty]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Roth |first=Andrew |author-link=Andrew Roth |title=Margaret Beckett |url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2001/mar/16/profiles.parliament1 |url-status=live |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=16 March 2001 |access-date=14 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151010213012/http://www.theguardian.com/politics/2001/mar/16/profiles.parliament1 |archive-date=10 October 2015}}</ref> She had two sisters, one later a nun, the other later a doctor and mother of three. She was educated at the [[Notre Dame High School, Norwich|Notre Dame High School for Girls]] in [[Norwich]], then at [[University of Manchester Institute of Science and Technology]], where she took a degree in [[metallurgy]].<ref name="Telegraph_educ">{{cite news |title=The Beckett files |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/1547189/The-Beckett-files.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/1547189/The-Beckett-files.html |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |access-date=29 January 2021 |work=The Telegraph |date=31 March 2007}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

Beckett was an active member of the Students' Union and served on its council. In 1961, she joined [[Associated Electrical Industries]] as a student apprentice in metallurgy. She also joined the [[Transport and General Workers Union]] in 1964. In 1966, she joined the [[University of Manchester]] as an experiment officer in its metallurgy department, and in 1970 went to work for the Labour Party as a researcher in [[industrial policy]].

==Member of Parliament==

In 1973, Beckett was selected as Labour candidate for [[Lincoln (constituency)|Lincoln]], which the party wanted to win back from ex-Labour MP [[Dick Taverne]], who had won the [[1973 Lincoln by-election|Lincoln by-election]] in March 1973 standing as the [[Democratic Labour Party (UK, 1972)|Democratic Labour]] candidate. At the [[February 1974 United Kingdom general election|February 1974 general election]], Beckett lost to Taverne by 1,297 votes. Following the election, she worked as a researcher for [[Judith Hart]], the [[Minister for Overseas Development]] at the Foreign Office. [[Harold Wilson]] called the [[October 1974 United Kingdom general election|October 1974  general election]], and Beckett again stood against Taverne in Lincoln. This time Beckett became the MP, with a majority of 984 votes. Almost immediately following her election she was appointed as Judith Hart's [[Parliamentary private secretary]]. Harold Wilson made her a [[Whip (politics)|Whip]] in 1975,<ref>{{cite news | title = New Whip appointed | page = 1 | newspaper = [[Liverpool Echo]] | date = 1975-01-27 | url = https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000271/19750127/004/0001 | access-date = 2023-11-01 | archive-date = 5 June 2024 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20240605033900/https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/account/register?countrykey=0&showgiftvoucherclaimingoptions=false&gift=false&nextpage=%2faccount%2flogin%3freturnurl%3d%252fviewer%252fbl%252f0000271%252f19750127%252f004%252f0001&rememberme=false&cookietracking=false&partnershipkey=0&newsletter=false&offers=false&registerreason=none&showsubscriptionoptions=false&showcouponmessaging=false&showfreetrialmessaging=false&showregisteroptions=false&showloginoptions=false&showcaptchaerrormessage=false&isonlyupgradeable=false | url-status = live }}{{subscription required | via = britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk}}</ref> promoted to [[Parliamentary under-secretary of state]] at the [[Department for Education and Skills (England)|Department of Education and Science]], replacing [[Joan Lestor]], who had resigned in protest over spending cuts.<ref>Benn Diaries, 11 March 1976</ref>

Beckett remained in that position until she lost her seat at the [[1979 United Kingdom general election|1979 general election]]. The [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] candidate [[Kenneth Carlisle]] narrowly won the seat with a 602-vote majority, the first time the Conservatives had won at Lincoln since [[1935 United Kingdom general election|1935]]. She joined [[Granada Television]] as a researcher in 1979. Out of Parliament, and now known as Margaret Beckett after her marriage, she was elected to Labour's [[National Executive Committee of the Labour Party (UK)|National Executive Committee]] in 1980, and supported the left-winger [[Tony Benn]] in the [[1981 Labour deputy leadership election]] narrowly won by [[Denis Healey]]. She was the subject of a vociferous attack by [[Joan Lestor]] at the conference. Beckett was selected to stand at the [[1983 United Kingdom general election|1983 general election]] as the Labour candidate in the parliamentary constituency of [[Derby South]] following the retirement of the sitting MP, [[Walter Johnson (politician)|Walter Johnson]]. At the election she retained the seat with a small majority of 421 votes. In March 2022, Beckett announced she would end her parliamentary career, standing down as MP for Derby South at the next general election.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Noble |first1=Samantha |last2=Roberts |first2=Georgia |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-derbyshire-60886091 |title=First female foreign secretary to retire as MP |publisher=[[BBC News]] |date=26 March 2022 |access-date=26 March 2022 |archive-date=26 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220326110049/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-derbyshire-60886091 |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Shadow Cabinet and Deputy Leader, 1984–1994===
{{see also|Beckett shadow cabinet}}
Upon returning to the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]], Beckett gradually moved away from the [[Left-wing politics|left]], supporting incumbent leader [[Neil Kinnock]] against Benn in 1988. By this time she was a front bencher, as a spokeswoman on Social Security since 1984, becoming a member of the [[shadow cabinet]] in 1989 as [[Shadow Chief Secretary to the Treasury]]. Following the [[1992 United Kingdom general election|1992 general election]] she was elected [[Deputy Leader of the Labour Party (UK)|Deputy Leader of the Labour Party]] and served under [[John Smith (Labour Party leader)|John Smith]] as [[Shadow Leader of the House of Commons]]. She became a [[Privy Council (United Kingdom)|Member of the Privy Council]] in 1993. She was the first woman to serve as deputy leader of the Labour Party.

Following the sudden death of [[John Smith (Labour Party leader)|John Smith]] from a heart attack on 12 May 1994, Beckett became Acting Leader of the Labour Party, the party's constitution providing for the automatic succession of the deputy leader for the remainder of the leadership term, upon the death or resignation of an incumbent leader in opposition. In times when the party is in opposition, party leaders are subject to annual reelection at the time of the annual party conference; accordingly, Beckett was constitutionally entitled to remain in office as acting leader until the 1994 Conference; however, the party's National Executive Committee (NEC) rapidly decided to bring forward the election for Labour Leader and Deputy Leader to July 1994.<ref name="BBC 12 May 04">{{cite news |title=Timeline: Blair's 10 years of leadership |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk_politics/3827555.stm |access-date=5 June 2024 |work=BBC News |publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation |date=19 May 2004 |language=en-GB |orig-date=First published 12 May 2004 |archive-date=20 September 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070920100443/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk_politics/3827555.stm |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="LabourList 19 Aug 21">{{cite news |last1=Pantelic |first1=Natasa |title=Margaret Beckett: "If you want to be at the table, you have to be in politics" |url=https://labourlist.org/2021/08/margaret-beckett-if-you-want-to-be-at-the-table-you-have-to-be-in-politics/ |access-date=5 June 2024 |work=[[LabourList]] |date=19 August 2021 |language=en-GB |archive-date=11 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220811052528/https://labourlist.org/2021/08/margaret-beckett-if-you-want-to-be-at-the-table-you-have-to-be-in-politics/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Beckett decided to run for the position of Labour Leader, but came last in [[1994 Labour Party leadership election|1994 leadership election]], behind [[Tony Blair]] and [[John Prescott]]. The deputy leadership was contested at the same time; Beckett was also defeated in this contest, coming second behind Prescott. Though she failed in both contests, she was retained in the shadow cabinet by Blair as [[Shadow Health Secretary]].<ref name="LabourList 19 Aug 21" /><ref name="Guardian 22 Jul 94">{{cite news |last1=White |first1=Michael |title=Blair starts revivalist crusade |url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/1994/jul/22/labour.uk1 |access-date=5 June 2024 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=22 July 1994 |language=en-GB |archive-date=5 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240605033853/https://www.theguardian.com/politics/1994/jul/22/labour.uk1 |url-status=live }}</ref>

A footnote to her ten-week tenure as caretaker leader of the Labour Party is that she was the leader at the time of the [[1994 European Parliament election in the United Kingdom|1994 European Parliament election]], which were held four weeks after she assumed the position. Labour's election campaign had been long in the planning under Smith, whose sudden death led to a "sympathy rise" in opinion polls for Labour, compounding what had already been a strong lead over the Conservatives. Consequently, Labour had a commanding victory in what was its best result in any of the four European elections held since 1979. The two Labour leadership elections followed six weeks later on 21 July 1994 and the Labour electorate did not appear to attribute any credit for the successful European election result to Beckett's chance-ordained position as acting leader in the four weeks immediately prior to the election.{{citation needed|date=November 2021}}

Under Blair's leadership, Beckett was the Shadow Secretary of State for [[Department of Health and Social Care|Health]], and then from 1995 the [[Shadow President of the Board of Trade]]. She was one of the leading critics of the government when the [[Scott Report]] published its findings into the [[Arms-to-Iraq]] scandal in 1996.{{citation needed|date=November 2021}} In [[2025 Labour Party deputy leadership election]], Beckett recalled that being deputy leader was a "ghastly job".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-09-10 |title='Being deputy Labour leader is a ghastly job' |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c0r0qnqp154o |access-date=2025-09-12 |website=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref>

===In government, 1997–2001===
The Labour Party was elected to government in a [[landslide victory|landslide]] in the [[1997 United Kingdom general election|1997 general election]] and Beckett held a number of senior positions in the [[First Blair ministry|Blair government]]. Following  the election she was appointed [[President of the Board of Trade]] (a position whose title later reverted to [[Secretary of State for Trade and Industry]]); the first woman to have held the post. She was succeeded by [[Peter Mandelson]] in July 1998.{{citation needed|date=November 2021}}

Beckett was then [[Leader of the House of Commons]] from 1998 until her replacement by [[Robin Cook]] in June 2001. Her tenure saw the introduction of [[Westminster Hall]] debates, which are debates held in a small chamber near Westminster Hall on topics of interest to individual MPs, committee reports, and other matters that would not ordinarily be debated in the Commons chamber.<ref>{{cite web |title=House of Commons Factsheet P4: Sittings of the House |url=http://www.parliament.uk/documents/upload/P04.pdf |url-status=dead |date=November 2006 |access-date=16 December 2007 |publisher=UK Parliament |page=2 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080529071521/http://www.parliament.uk/documents/upload/P04.pdf |archive-date=29 May 2008}}</ref> Debates that take place in Westminster Hall are often more consensual and informal, and can address the concerns of [[backbencher]]s. She received admiration for her work as Leader of the House,<ref name=MargProf>{{cite news |title=Profile: Margaret Beckett |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/4977348.stm |url-status=live |publisher=BBC News |date=5 May 2006 |access-date=27 April 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk_politics/4977348.stm |archive-date=30 June 2009 |df=dmy}}{{failed verification|date=August 2009}}</ref> working on this and a number of other elements of the Labour government's modernisation agenda for Parliament. In 2000, she expressed republican sympathies.<ref>{{cite news |last=Cracknell |first=David |title=Prescott and Beckett fuel Labour split on monarchy |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/1346189/Prescott-and-Beckett-fuel-Labour-split-on-monarchy.html |url-status=live |work=The Telegraph |date=2 July 2000 |access-date=25 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160920073720/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/1346189/Prescott-and-Beckett-fuel-Labour-split-on-monarchy.html |archive-date=20 September 2016}}</ref>

===Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, 2001–2006===
[[File:Official portrait of Margaret Beckett as Environment Secretary.jpg|thumb|Beckett as [[Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs|Environment Secretary]]]]
Following the [[2001 United Kingdom general election|2001 general election]], Beckett became Secretary of State at the new [[Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs]] (DEFRA), created after the [[Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food]] (MAFF) was abolished in the wake of perceived mismanagement of the [[foot-and-mouth]] [[2001 United Kingdom foot-and-mouth outbreak|epidemic in 2001]]. The new department also incorporated some of the functions of the former [[Department for the Environment, Transport and the Regions]] (DETR).

Beckett rejected demands for an expansion of [[Nuclear power in the United Kingdom|nuclear power]] from a lobby including energy minister [[Brian Wilson (Labour politician)|Brian Wilson]] and Downing Street staff. She argued there was no need for new nuclear for at least 15 years given current energy prices and generation capacity. The 2003 energy [[white paper]] stated that "the current economics of nuclear power make it unattractive" and there were no proposals for new nuclear power stations.<ref name=guardian-20040919>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2004/sep/19/nuclear.greenpolitics |title=Beckett rejects nuclear option |work=The Guardian |date=19 September 2004 |access-date=25 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190225223539/https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2004/sep/19/nuclear.greenpolitics |archive-date=25 February 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=telegraph-20050508>{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/1489561/Beckett-puts-block-on-the-building-of-new-nuclear-power-stations.html |title=Beckett puts block on the building of new nuclear power stations |author1=Robert Watts |author2=Andrew Murray-Watson |work=The Telegraph |date=8 May 2005 |access-date=25 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190225162009/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/1489561/Beckett-puts-block-on-the-building-of-new-nuclear-power-stations.html |archive-date=25 February 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=bower-2016>{{cite book |pages=297–304 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JR5xCwAAQBAJ |title=Broken Vows : Tony Blair : the Tragedy of Power |last=Bower |first=Tom |publisher=[[Faber and Faber]] |year=2016 |isbn=9780571314201 |via=Google Books |access-date=25 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190225163041/https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=JR5xCwAAQBAJ |archive-date=25 February 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Beckett held the position of [[Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs]] until May 2006, when she was succeeded by [[David Miliband]]. Beckett was on the front line of the government's efforts to tackle [[climate change]], and attended international conferences on the matter.{{citation needed|date=November 2021}} In a report published on 29 March 2007 by the [[Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Select Committee]], she was criticised for her role in the failures of the [[Rural Payments Agency]] when she had been Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.<ref>{{cite news |last=Clover |first=Charles |title=Beckett should be sacked over farm payments fiasco, say MPs |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/main.jhtml?xml=/news/2007/03/29/nfarms29.xml |work=The Telegraph |date=30 March 2007 |access-date=2 April 2007 |archive-date=30 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/main.jhtml?xml=%2Fnews%2F2007%2F03%2F29%2Fnfarms29.xml |url-status=dead |df=dmy}}</ref>

===Foreign Secretary: 2006–2007===
Following the [[2006 United Kingdom local elections|2006 local elections]], Blair demoted [[Foreign Secretary (United Kingdom)|Foreign Secretary]] [[Jack Straw]], and appointed Beckett as Straw's successor. She was the first woman to hold the post, and only the second woman (after [[Margaret Thatcher]]) to hold one of the [[Great Offices of State]].

Some commentators claim that Beckett was promoted to Foreign Secretary because she was considered to be a 'safe pair of hands' and a loyal member of the Cabinet.<ref>{{cite news |title=UK has first woman foreign secretary |url=http://articles.cnn.com/2006-05-05/world/britain.beckett_1_labour-party-iraq-war-local-council-elections?_s=PM:WORLD |publisher=[[CNN]] |date=5 May 2006 |access-date=20 March 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://articles.cnn.com/2006-05-05/world/britain.beckett_1_labour-party-iraq-war-local-council-elections?_s=PM%3AWORLD |archive-date=30 June 2009 |url-status=dead |df=dmy}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Media Strategy Guide to Cabinet Reshuffle |url=http://www.euronanotrade.com/index.php?option=content&task=view&id=459&Itemid=71 |url-status=dead |work=Euro Nano Trade Alliance |access-date=20 March 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://www.euronanotrade.com/index.php?option=content&task=view&id=459&Itemid=71 |archive-date=30 June 2009 |df=dmy}}</ref> Her experience at DEFRA in dealing with international climate change issues has also been cited as a factor in the move.{{citation needed|date=November 2021}}

Beckett had to adapt quickly to her diplomatic role; within a few hours of her appointment as Foreign Secretary, she flew to the [[United Nations]] in New York City for an urgent meeting of foreign ministers to discuss the [[Iran]] nuclear weapons crisis. About a month later, she came under fire for not responding quickly enough to the [[2006 Lebanon War]] which saw [[Israel]] invade that country, although some reports suggested that the delay was caused by Cabinet division rather than Beckett's reluctance to make a public statement on the matter.<ref>{{cite news |last=Assinder |first=Nick |title=Commons Confidential: November 2006 |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/6207306.stm |url-status=live |publisher=BBC News |date=4 December 2006 |access-date=20 March 2007 |archive-date=19 February 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070219124000/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk_politics/6207306.stm |df=dmy}}</ref>

[[File:Beckett Rice.jpg|thumb|250px|Beckett appears with [[US Secretary of State]], [[Condoleezza Rice]], following her appointment as Foreign Secretary]]

Beckett is understood{{by whom|date=November 2021}} to have delegated European issues to the [[Foreign Office]] minister responsible for Europe, [[Geoff Hoon]], who, following his demotion as Defence Secretary, continued to attend Cabinet meetings. Hoon and Beckett were said to have a difficult ministerial relationship.<ref>{{cite journal |date=February 2007 |url=http://www.prospect-magazine.co.uk/article_details.php?id=8234 |title=Brussels Diary |access-date=20 March 2007 |journal=Prospect |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://www.prospect-magazine.co.uk/article_details.php?id=8234 |archive-date=30 June 2009 |url-status=dead |df=dmy}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Carlin |first=Brendan |title=Hoon uses Beckett's absence to reopen issue of EU's future |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/main.jhtml?xml=/news/2006/11/03/npolitics103.xml |url-status=dead |work=The Telegraph |date=3 November 2006 |access-date=20 March 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/main.jhtml?xml=%2Fnews%2F2006%2F11%2F03%2Fnpolitics103.xml |archive-date=30 June 2009 |df=dmy}}</ref> As Foreign Secretary, Beckett came in for some trenchant criticism. According to ''[[The Times]]'', she did not stand up well in comparison with the previous Foreign Secretary, [[Jack Straw]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Rees-Mogg |first=William |author-link=William Rees-Mogg |title=Being beastly to Beckett |url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/comment/columnists/william_rees_mogg/article676216.ece |url-status=dead |work=Times Online |date=19 June 2006 |access-date=31 October 2006 |archive-date=30 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/comment/columnists/william_rees_mogg/article676216.ece |df=dmy}}</ref> ''[[The Spectator]]'' described her as "at heart, an old, isolationist, pacifist Leftist" and called on her to resign,<ref>{{cite web |last=Heffer |first=Simon |author-link=Simon Heffer |title=Not up to the job |url=http://www.spectator.co.uk/online-edition/elsewhere/24342/not-up-to-the-job.thtml |work=[[The Spectator]] |date=2 August 2006 |access-date=31 October 2006}} {{dead link|date=April 2014}}</ref> and the ''[[New Statesman]]'' accused her of allowing the Foreign Office to become subservient to 10 Downing Street after the tenures of Straw and [[Robin Cook]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Riddell |first1=Mary |last2=Kampfner |first2=John |author-link1=Mary Riddell |author-link2=John Kampfner |title=Interview: Margaret Beckett |url=http://www.newstatesman.com/200612180059 |url-status=dead |work=[[New Statesman]] |date=18 December 2006 |access-date=27 March 2007 |archive-date=30 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://www.newstatesman.com/200612180059 |df=dmy}}</ref>

In August 2006, 37 Labour Party members in her Derby South constituency left the party and joined the [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrats]], criticising her approach to the [[2006 Lebanon War|Israeli invasion of Lebanon]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Beckett suffers Labour defections |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/5285986.stm |url-status=live |publisher=BBC News |date=25 August 2006 |access-date=31 October 2006 |archive-date=30 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/5285986.stm |df=dmy}}</ref> Two weeks earlier, Beckett's successor, [[David Miliband]], raised concerns during a cabinet meeting about the failure of Blair and Beckett to call for an immediate ceasefire.<ref name=no10rebuff>{{cite news |title=No 10 'rebuffed hostilities call' |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk_politics/5234590.stm |url-status=live |publisher=BBC News |date=2 August 2006 |access-date=30 June 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/5234590.stm |archive-date=30 June 2009 |df=dmy}}</ref> Straw and [[Hilary Benn]], then [[International Development Secretary]], also raised concerns. Former minister [[Michael Meacher]] said there was "despair, anger and bewilderment" in the Labour Party at the UK's failure to call for an immediate ceasefire.<ref name=no10rebuff/>

===Post-Blair years===
Upon taking office as prime minister, [[Gordon Brown]] made it known that Beckett would not continue as foreign secretary.<ref>{{cite news |title=Beckett out as Foreign Secretary |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/6246832.stm |url-status=live |publisher=BBC News |date=27 June 2007 |access-date=24 July 2008 |archive-date=30 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk_politics/6246832.stm |df=dmy}}</ref> On 28 June 2007, Brown selected David Miliband as her replacement<ref>{{cite news |title=Cabinet at a glance |url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2007/jun/28/labour.uk1 |date=28 June 2007 |access-date=28 June 2007 |work=The Guardian |archive-date=30 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://politics.guardian.co.uk/gordonbrown/story/0%2C%2C2113987%2C00.html |url-status=live |df=dmy}}</ref> and Beckett returned to the back benches. It was announced on 29 January 2008 that Beckett would become the new head of the Prime Minister's [[Intelligence and Security Committee]], replacing [[Paul Murphy, Baron Murphy of Torfaen|Paul Murphy]], who became the [[Secretary of State for Wales]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Beckett to head security watchdog |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/7215925.stm |url-status=live |publisher=BBC News |date=29 January 2008 |access-date=29 January 2008 |archive-date=30 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk_politics/7215925.stm |df=dmy}}</ref>

Having been tipped for a possible return to the front bench in July 2008, due to her reputation as a solid media performer,<ref>{{cite news |last=Webster |first=Philip |title=Margaret Beckett tipped for a Cabinet comeback |url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/news/politics/article4387167.ece |work=Times Online |date=24 July 2008 |access-date=24 July 2008}}{{dead link|date=September 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> Beckett returned to government in the [[reshuffle]] on 3 October 2008 as the [[Minister of State for Housing]] in the [[Department for Communities and Local Government]]. She attended Cabinet meetings, but was not a full member and was not to be entitled to vote on collective decisions. She ultimately was allowed to return due to her cabinet experience and her economic management in the past.{{citation needed|date=November 2021}} Beckett was a member of the [[Top Level Group|Top Level Group of UK Parliamentarians for Multilateral Nuclear Disarmament and Non-proliferation]], established in October 2009.<ref>{{cite news |last=Borger |first=Julian |title=Nuclear-free world ultimate aim of new cross-party pressure group |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2009/sep/08/nuclear-disarmament-cross-party-group |url-status=dead |work=The Guardian |date=8 September 2009 |archive-date=30 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://www.guardian.co.uk/world/2009/sep/08/nuclear-disarmament-cross-party-group |df=dmy}}</ref> She has served as a member of the [[Henry Jackson Society]] Advisory Council.<ref name="guardian-20130520">{{cite news |last=Bloodworth |first=James |title=Labour should cut its ties with the illiberal Henry Jackson Society |url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2013/may/20/labour-cut-ties-henry-jackson-society |work=The Guardian |date=20 May 2013 |access-date=8 August 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160812183140/https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2013/may/20/labour-cut-ties-henry-jackson-society |archive-date=12 August 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="hjs-20160808">{{cite web |url=http://henryjacksonsociety.org/people/council-members/ |title=Advisory Council |publisher=Henry Jackson Society |access-date=8 August 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130923022301/http://henryjacksonsociety.org/people/council-members/ |archive-date=23 September 2013}}</ref>

===Expenses===
{{main|United Kingdom parliamentary expenses scandal}}

Beckett was found to have claimed £600 for [[hanging basket]]s and [[pot plant]]s by ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'' in the [[2009 expenses scandal]]. As she had no [[mortgage]] or [[renting|rent]] outstanding it was queried how she managed to claim £72,537 between 2004 and 2008 on a house in her constituency when she was renting out her London flat and living in a [[grace and favour]] flat.<ref>{{cite news |last=Rayner |first=Gordon |title=Margaret Beckett's £600 claim for hanging baskets and pot plants: MPs expenses |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/newstopics/mps-expenses/5293973/Margaret-Becketts-600-claim-for-hanging-baskets-and-pot-plants-MPs-expenses.html |url-status=dead |work=The Telegraph |date=8 May 2009 |access-date=5 April 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/newstopics/mps-expenses/5293973/Margaret-Becketts-600-claim-for-hanging-baskets-and-pot-plants-MPs-expenses.html |archive-date=30 June 2009 |df=dmy}}</ref>

===Bid to become Speaker===
On 10 June 2009, Beckett announced that she wished to replace [[Michael Martin, Baron Martin of Springburn|Michael Martin]] as [[Speaker of the House of Commons (United Kingdom)|Speaker of the House of Commons]]. She said: "I think at the moment we have got very considerable problems in Parliament. We have got to make changes.... After the next election, if we have a more finely balanced chamber than we have had in the recent past, it will be a very different ball game.... I hope I can help us deal with that." Beckett received 74 votes in the first round and 70 votes in the second round of the 2009 Speaker election, reaching the third place as the strongest Labour candidate both times but considerably trailing the two Conservative frontrunners [[John Bercow]] and [[George Young, Baron Young of Cookham|George Young]]. She withdrew following the second round of voting.<ref>{{cite web |title=Election of the Speaker: Latest |url=http://news.parliament.uk/2009/06/election-of-the-speaker-latest/ |publisher=UK Parliament |date=22 June 2009 |access-date=29 April 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://news.parliament.uk/2009/06/election-of-the-speaker-latest/ |archive-date=30 June 2009 |url-status=dead |df=dmy}}</ref> In August 2009, Beckett wrote to Sir Christopher Kelly, Chairman of the [[Committee on Standards in Public Life]] which was investigating MPs' expenses. In the letter, she says the allowances do not adequately cover MPs' costs, which include political campaigns. ''The Telegraph'' criticised the "self-pitying" letter, saying it will fuel "concern that some MPs are not genuinely committed to reform".<ref>{{cite news |last=Oakeshott |first=Isabel |author-link=Isabel Oakeshott |title=Margaret Beckett in 'take pity' plea on expenses |url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/news/politics/article6806398.ece |work=Times Online |date=23 August 2009 |access-date=23 August 2009}}{{dead link|date=September 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

===Alternative Vote referendum===
On 26 November 2010, Beckett was announced as the President of the [[NOtoAV]] campaign, which campaigned to retain the [[First Past the Post]] (FPTP) electoral system at the [[2011 United Kingdom Alternative Vote referendum]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Labour veterans to oppose change to AV election system |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-11837428 |url-status=dead |publisher=BBC News |date=26 November 2010 |access-date=26 November 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-11837428 |archive-date=30 June 2009 |df=dmy}}</ref> She led the campaign to success, and FPTP remains the system used in UK parliamentary elections.

===2015 Labour leadership election===
Beckett was one of 36 Labour MPs to nominate [[Jeremy Corbyn]] as a candidate in the [[2015 Labour Party leadership election (UK)|Labour leadership election of 2015]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Who nominated who for the 2015 Labour leadership election?|url=http://www.newstatesman.com/politics/2015/06/who-nominated-who-2015-labour-leadership-election|access-date=21 January 2016|work=New Statesman|date=15 June 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180628072303/https://www.newstatesman.com/politics/2015/06/who-nominated-who-2015-labour-leadership-election|archive-date=28 June 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> Later, during an interview with [[BBC Radio 4]]'s ''The [[World at One]]'', after it became known he was in the lead among the candidates, Beckett was asked if she was "a moron" for nominating Corbyn. She replied: "I am one of them."<ref>{{cite news|title=Margaret Beckett: I was moron to nominate Jeremy Corbyn|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-33625612|access-date=21 January 2016|publisher=BBC News|date=22 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304103908/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-33625612|archive-date=4 March 2016|url-status=live}}</ref> In January 2016, Beckett claimed that Labour would need an "unexpected political miracle" if it were to win under his leadership,<ref>{{cite news|last=Elliott|first=Francis|title=Corbyn needs miracle to win, says Beckett as report draws fire|url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/article/corbyn-needs-miracle-to-win-says-beckett-as-report-draws-fire-zwwkkwfwl7c|access-date=21 January 2016|work=[[The Times]]|date=20 January 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160120170447/http://www.thetimes.co.uk/tto/news/politics/article4669948.ece|archive-date=20 January 2016|url-status=live |url-access=subscription}}</ref> and criticised Corbyn for failing to win back the trust of the electorate on [[welfare reform]] and [[mass immigration]], saying: "I think we had the right policies towards immigration, but the simple thuggishness of the kind of Ukip and Conservative approach is easier to understand and we didn't overcome those communication difficulties ... We have to try and work on ways to overcome that – I'm not suggesting we've done it yet".<ref>{{cite news|last=Stone|first=Jon|title=Jeremy Corbyn hasn't won back the public's trust on welfare and immigration, says Margaret Beckett|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/jeremy-corbyn-hasnt-won-back-the-publics-trust-on-welfare-and-immigration-says-margaret-beckett-a6822306.html|access-date=21 January 2016|work=[[The Independent]]|date=20 January 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160124091020/http://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/jeremy-corbyn-hasnt-won-back-the-publics-trust-on-welfare-and-immigration-says-margaret-beckett-a6822306.html|archive-date=24 January 2016|url-status=live}}</ref> She later supported [[Owen Smith]] in the failed attempt to replace Corbyn in the [[2016 Labour Party leadership election (UK)|2016 Labour leadership election]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://labourlist.org/2016/07/which-mps-and-meps-have-nominated-owen-smith/|title=Full list of MPs and MEPs backing challenger Owen Smith|date=2016-07-21|website=LabourList|language=en-GB|access-date=2019-07-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190715214543/https://labourlist.org/2016/07/which-mps-and-meps-have-nominated-owen-smith/|archive-date=15 July 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> In February 2019, she acknowledged during an interview with [[Sophy Ridge]] on [[Sky News]] that she was "surprised" about how Corbyn had "grown into the job" after taking on the leadership. She further claimed that veteran Conservative MP [[Kenneth Clarke]] called Corbyn a "perfectly competent" opposition leader.<ref name="Bartlett 2019">{{cite web | last=Bartlett | first=Nicola | title=John McDonnell warns splitting Labour could keep the Tories in for a decade | website=mirror | date=2019-02-17 | url=https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/politics/john-mcdonnell-warns-splitting-labour-14010978 | access-date=2022-08-10 | archive-date=10 August 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220810142142/https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/politics/john-mcdonnell-warns-splitting-labour-14010978 | url-status=live }}</ref>

===Beckett report===
On 16 January 2016, Beckett released "Learning the Lessons from Defeat Taskforce Report", a 35-page report into why the Labour Party lost the [[2015 United Kingdom general election|2015 general election]] after the then deputy leader [[Harriet Harman]] requested Beckett investigate the reasons for Labour's failure.<ref>{{cite news |last=Goodfellow |first=Mollie |title=Why Labour lost the election. In its own words |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/the-beckett-report-into-labours-election-loss-has-finally-been-released-a6821406.html |url-status=live |work=The Independent |date=19 January 2016 |access-date=21 January 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160119203534/http://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/the-beckett-report-into-labours-election-loss-has-finally-been-released-a6821406.html |archive-date=19 January 2016}}</ref> Labour's defeat came as a shock to pollsters, whose polls had suggested that the result would be much closer than it eventually was. Ultimately, the Conservatives won a narrow majority.<ref name="Beckett Report" />

The report said that explanations including Labour being "anti-business" or "anti-aspiration" were not "significant" factors, saying that "reasons for defeat should be treated with caution and require deeper analysis".<ref name="Beckett Report">{{cite news|last=Stone|first=Jon|title=Forget what you think you know about why Labour lost the election|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/commonly-believed-reasons-why-labour-lost-the-election-arent-significant-says-partys-beckett-report-a6821476.html|access-date=21 January 2016|work=The Independent|date=19 January 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160122024003/http://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/commonly-believed-reasons-why-labour-lost-the-election-arent-significant-says-partys-beckett-report-a6821476.html|archive-date=22 January 2016|url-status=live}}</ref> The main reasons given for Labour's losses were the perceived weakness of [[Ed Miliband]] as party leader, fear of Labour's relationship with the [[Scottish National Party]] (SNP) among English voters, a perceived association with [[2008 financial crisis|the financial crisis]] under the [[Brown ministry]],<ref name="Beckett Report"/> and "issues of connection" with voters.<ref>{{cite news |last=Mason |first=Rowena |title=Beckett report: Labour lost election over economy, immigration and benefits |url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2016/jan/14/beckett-report-labour-lost-2015-election-economy-immigrants-benefits |url-status=live |work=The Guardian |date=14 January 2016 |access-date=21 January 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160117031140/http://www.theguardian.com/politics/2016/jan/14/beckett-report-labour-lost-2015-election-economy-immigrants-benefits |archive-date=17 January 2016}}</ref> The report also said that it would be difficult for Labour to win next time because of changes to constituency boundaries ([[2013 periodic review of Westminster constituencies|due in 2018]]), voter registration changes and restrictions on trade union funding of parties. Beckett said the party should campaign in ordinary language, focus its policy on the condition of Britain in 2020, unite for the [[2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum|2016 European Union membership referendum]], and draw up a five-year media strategy.<ref name="Beckett Report" />

The Beckett report was criticised by some on the left wing of British politics as "show[ing] that many Labour politicians still don't really understand why they lost" and blaming factors such as the rise of the SNP on Labour's losses, rather than campaigning against [[United Kingdom government austerity programme|austerity]].<ref name="Socialist Worker">{{cite news|last=Clark|first=Nick|title=Beckett report can't work out how Labour lost in 2015|url=https://socialistworker.co.uk/art/42037/Beckett+report+cant+work+out+how+Labour+lost+in+2015|access-date=21 January 2016|work=Socialist Worker (Britain)|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160122162934/https://socialistworker.co.uk/art/42037/Beckett+report+cant+work+out+how+Labour+lost+in+2015|archive-date=22 January 2016|url-status=live}}</ref> Others criticised the report for being too broad and too vague in its conclusions. [[Stephen Bush]] wrote in the ''New Statesman'' that "every bit of the Labour party will have something it can cling to" in the report:<ref name="Stephen Bush">{{cite news |last=Bush |first=Stephen |author-link=Stephen Bush |title=The Beckett Report won't help Labour win the next election |url=http://www.newstatesman.com/politics/elections/2016/01/beckett-report-wont-help-labour-win-next-election |work=New Statesman |date=19 January 2016 |access-date=21 January 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160120091411/http://www.newstatesman.com/politics/elections/2016/01/beckett-report-wont-help-labour-win-next-election |archive-date=20 January 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref> He continued:
{{blockquote|Supporters of [[Jeremy Corbyn]] will take heart from the fact that individual left-wing policies, like the mansion tax, were popular. But Corbyn-sceptics will note that it was voters that went for [[Tony Blair]] and [[David Cameron]] that failed to back the party in 2015, which they will take as an endorsement of a centrist approach. Ed Miliband's diehard supporters – they do exist, believe it or not – will see the report as an endorsement of the Miliband era policy approach but will argue that a more convincing frontman would have sealed the deal.<ref name="Stephen Bush" />}}

[[Owen Jones]], a columnist for ''[[The Guardian]]'', said that the left should not fear the Beckett report, saying: "Let's have a full inquest, not in the interests of navel-gazing, but in the interests of winning."<ref>{{cite news |last=Jones |first=Owen |author-link=Owen Jones |title=The left must not fear the Beckett report – it will help Labour win power |url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2016/jan/18/labour-beckett-report-left-election-defeat-2015 |url-status=live |work=The Guardian |date=18 January 2016 |access-date=21 January 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160120211727/http://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2016/jan/18/labour-beckett-report-left-election-defeat-2015 |archive-date=20 January 2016}}</ref> According to the ''[[Morning Star (British newspaper)|Morning Star]]'', many centrist and more right-wing Labour politicians also welcomed the report.<ref>{{cite news |title=Set little store by Beckett |url=http://www.morningstaronline.co.uk/a-7bbd-Set-little-store-by-Beckett |url-status=dead |work=[[Morning Star (British newspaper)|Morning Star]] |date=15 January 2016 |access-date=22 January 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160128175612/http://www.morningstaronline.co.uk/a-7bbd-Set-little-store-by-Beckett |archive-date=28 January 2016 |df=dmy-all}}</ref> In Parliament, Beckett is Chair of the National Security Strategy (Joint Committee), and is a former member of the Intelligence and Security Committee of Parliament and Modernisation of the House of Commons Committee.<ref>{{cite web |title=Margaret Beckett MP |url=https://www.parliament.uk/biographies/commons/margaret-beckett/328 |url-status=live |publisher=UK Parliament |access-date=28 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190328120300/https://www.parliament.uk/biographies/commons/margaret-beckett/328 |archive-date=28 March 2019}}</ref>

=== National Executive Committee chairmanship ===
On 24 November 2020, Beckett was elected to succeed the [[Transport Salaried Staffs' Association]]'s Andi Fox as the Chair of the Labour Party's National Executive Committee. She was elected unopposed after NEC members from the left of the party staged a virtual walkout, protesting her election over then vice-chair Ian Murray from the [[Fire Brigades Union]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Rodgers|first=Sienna|title=Margaret Beckett elected as NEC chair after left stage digital walkout|date=24 November 2020|url=https://labourlist.org/2020/11/margaret-beckett-elected-as-nec-chair-after-left-stage-digital-walk-out/|access-date=6 January 2021|website=LabourList|language=en-GB|archive-date=26 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210126131206/https://labourlist.org/2020/11/margaret-beckett-elected-as-nec-chair-after-left-stage-digital-walk-out/|url-status=live}}</ref> Beckett was criticised after being overheard insulting a fellow NEC member during a [[Zoom (software)|Zoom]] call on 11 March 2021. Beckett thought her microphone was turned off when calling [[Laura Pidcock]] a "silly cow", after which Pidcock left the meeting.<ref name="Rodgers">{{cite web|last=Rodgers|first=Sienna|date=12 March 2021|title=Scrutiny of the Metropolitan Police and women's fight to #ReclaimTheseStreets|url=https://labourlist.org/2021/03/scrutiny-of-the-metropolitan-police-and-womens-fight-to-reclaimthesestreets/|access-date=12 March 2021|website=LabourList|language=en-GB|archive-date=12 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210312125248/https://labourlist.org/2021/03/scrutiny-of-the-metropolitan-police-and-womens-fight-to-reclaimthesestreets/|url-status=live}}</ref> Beckett apologised immediately and told the BBC the following day: "I deeply regret the remark, which was unjustifiable."<ref name="BBC 12 March">{{cite news |title=Labour MP Margaret Beckett apologises over 'silly cow' remark |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-56376710 |last=Scott |first=Jennifer |date=12 March 2021 |publisher=BBC News |access-date=12 March 2021 |archive-date=12 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210312140646/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-56376710 |url-status=live }}</ref> Fellow NEC members called on her to resign, while Labour's general secretary [[David Evans, Baron Evans of Sealand|David Evans]] said that complaints against Beckett would be investigated.<ref name="Rodgers" />

==Honours==
Beckett was sworn of the [[Privy Council (United Kingdom)|Privy Council]] in 1993. She was appointed [[Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (DBE) in the [[2013 New Year Honours]] for public and political service<ref>{{London Gazette |issue=60367 |date=29 December 2012 |page=6 |supp=y}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=New Year Honours: Margaret Beckett and Richard Shepherd on list |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-20858556 |url-status=dead |publisher=[[BBC News]] |date=28 December 2012 |access-date=29 December 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-20858556 |archive-date=30 June 2009 |df=dmy}}</ref> and was promoted to [[Dame Grand Cross of the Order of the British Empire]] (GBE) in the [[2024 New Year Honours]] for parliamentary, political and public service.<ref>{{London Gazette |issue=64269 |supp=y |page=N8 |date=30 December 2023}}</ref> In November 2017, she was awarded the [[honorary degree]] of [[Doctor of the University]] (DUniv) from the [[University of Derby]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.derby.ac.uk/about/honorary-awards/honorands/margaret-beckett/|title=Dame Margaret Beckett|publisher=Derby University|access-date=28 February 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190222151854/https://www.derby.ac.uk/about/honorary-awards/honorands/margaret-beckett/|archive-date=22 February 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> After standing down as an MP, Beckett was nominated for a [[life peer]]age in the [[2024 Dissolution Honours]].<ref>{{London Gazette |date=7 August 2024 |issue=64480 |page=15222 |supp=y}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Dissolution Peerages 2024 |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/dissolution-peerages-2024 |access-date=4 July 2024 |website=GOV.UK |language=en |archive-date=4 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240704204232/https://www.gov.uk/government/news/dissolution-peerages-2024 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Whannel |first=Kate |date=4 July 2024 |title=Theresa May and 'bionic' MP awarded peerages |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c84975xgdwlo |work=BBC News |language=en |access-date=4 July 2024 |archive-date=1 October 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241001051354/https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c84975xgdwlo |url-status=live }}</ref> She was created ''Baroness Beckett, of Old Normanton in the City of Derby'', on 14 August 2024.<ref>{{London Gazette |date=20 August 2024 |issue=64493 |page=16086}}</ref>

==Personal life==
She married the chairman of her local [[Constituency Labour Party]], Lionel "Leo" Beckett (born 1926), in August 1979.<ref name=MargProf/><ref>{{cite news |last=Coates |first=Sam |author-link=Sam Coates |title=Taxpayers foot the bill for globetrotting Mr Beckett |url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/news/politics/article629076.ece |work=Times Online |date=8 November 2006 |access-date=28 August 2009}}{{dead link|date=September 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref><ref name=LeoObit>{{cite news | last=Hudson |first=Lucian | title=Leo Beckett obituary | work=The Guardian | url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2022/feb/13/leo-beckett-obituary | date=13 February 2022 | accessdate=16 June 2023}}</ref> Beckett employed her husband as her office manager, on a salary up to £30,000.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theipsa.org.uk/mp-costs/your-mp/margaret-beckett/|title=Margaret Beckett|publisher=IPSA|access-date=28 March 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170613022211/http://www.theipsa.org.uk/mp-costs/your-mp/margaret-beckett/|archive-date=13 June 2017|url-status=live}}</ref> The practice of MPs employing family members has been criticised by some sections of the media on the lines that it promotes [[nepotism]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/newstopics/mps-expenses/11706561/One-in-four-MPs-employs-a-family-member-the-full-list-revealed.html|title=One in five MPs employs a family member: the full list revealed|date=29 June 2015|work=The Telegraph|access-date=28 March 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170402065627/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/newstopics/mps-expenses/11706561/One-in-four-MPs-employs-a-family-member-the-full-list-revealed.html|archive-date=2 April 2017|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Mason |first=Rowena |title=Keeping it in the family: new MPs continue to hire relatives as staff |url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2015/jun/29/mps-continue-hire-relatives-as-staff |url-status=live |work=The Guardian |date=29 June 2015 |access-date=28 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180810142533/https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2015/jun/29/mps-continue-hire-relatives-as-staff |archive-date=10 August 2018}}</ref> Although MPs who were first elected in [[2017 United Kingdom general election|2017]] have been banned from employing family members, the restriction is not retroactive.<ref>{{cite news |title=MPs banned from employing spouses after election in expenses crackdown |url=https://www.standard.co.uk/news/politics/mps-banned-from-employing-spouses-after-election-in-expenses-crackdown-a3520036.html |url-status=live |work=Evening Standard |date=21 April 2017 |access-date=28 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181225210938/https://www.standard.co.uk/news/politics/mps-banned-from-employing-spouses-after-election-in-expenses-crackdown-a3520036.html |archive-date=25 December 2018}}</ref> Leo Beckett had two sons from a previous marriage, and three grandchildren. Beckett and her husband enjoyed caravan holidays <ref>{{cite web |title=MP picks up the keys to 2011 Bailey Pegasus caravan |url=http://www.caravantimes.co.uk/news/makes/bailey/pegasus/mp-picks-up-the-keys-to-2011-bailey-pegasus-caravan-$21378194.htm |url-status=live |work=Caravan Times |date=20 September 2010 |access-date=13 October 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923200425/http://www.caravantimes.co.uk/news/makes/bailey/pegasus/mp-picks-up-the-keys-to-2011-bailey-pegasus-caravan-$21378194.htm |archive-date=23 September 2015}}</ref>  throughout her political career.<ref>{{cite news |title=Follow that caravan – this is a job for special branch |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/1524898/Follow-that-caravan-this-is-a-job-for-special-branch.html |url-status=dead |work=The Telegraph |date=27 July 2006 |access-date=28 August 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/1524898/Follow-that-caravan-this-is-a-job-for-special-branch.html |archive-date=30 June 2009 |df=dmy}}</ref> Leo Beckett died in 2021 at the age of 95.<ref>{{cite news | title=Dame Margaret Beckett's husband Leo dies, aged 95 | work=BBC News | url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-derbyshire-59649266 | date=14 December 2021 | accessdate=16 June 2023 | archive-date=16 June 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230616111905/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-derbyshire-59649266 | url-status=live }}</ref>
